Christoph Pezel
kris'tof pet'sel
n. (Christoph Pezel, 1539–1604, Philippist expelled from Wittenberg, who brought the city of Bremen to the Reformed confession)
Pezel, a south German surname, probably a diminutive of Peter; Christoph, from Greek Christophoros, one who bears Christ.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Christoph Pezel was a professor at Wittenberg of the party called Philippist, which followed Melanchthon in holding a doctrine of the Lord's Supper nearer the Reformed than the Lutheran. When the Elector of Saxony turned against that party in 1574 Pezel was imprisoned and then expelled, with others, in the affair the Lutheran historians call the crypto-Calvinist crisis; it was the moment at which Lutheranism closed its ranks and the Philippists had to become Reformed or be silent. Pezel went to Nassau, served the counts there, and in 1581 was called to Bremen, where he spent the rest of his life. Bremen had been Lutheran, and under Pezel's teaching and preaching the city went over, formally and gradually, to the Reformed confession; he drew up the Bremen Consensus of 1595, which set out that position, and he founded the city's gymnasium illustre, which trained its ministers thereafter. He died in 1604. The dictionary enters Pezel because the Philippists are a lost party worth remembering: men who believed they were being faithful to Melanchthon and to the Augsburg Confession rightly read, who were thrown out for it, and who found when they looked for a home that the only church which would confess what they already held was the Reformed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a consensus as agreement, concurrence; to expel as to drive out, to banish; and a party as a number of persons united in opinion.

expand to see more

CONSENT, n. [L. consensus.] Agreement of minds; accord; concurrence; unity of opinion.

EXPEL, v.t. [L. expello.] To drive or force out; to eject; to banish; to exclude from a society or community.

PARTY, n. [Fr. partie.] A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community.

CRYPTO, a Greek prefix signifying hidden or secret; used in composition, as crypto-Calvinist, a secret Calvinist.

GRADUAL, adj. [L. gradus, a step.] Proceeding by steps or degrees; advancing step by step; slow.

Modern Corruption

Wittenberg Philippist expelled in 1574 who brought Bremen to the Reformed confession, drew its Consensus of 1595 and founded its high school.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary states plainly where it stands on the quarrel that made Pezel. The Philippists held that Christ is present in the Supper to the faith of the believer and not in, with and under the elements to the mouth of all; that is the Reformed doctrine, and it is the dictionary's. The charge of crypto-Calvinism was therefore substantially accurate, and the fault in the proceeding was not the identification but the method: imprisonment and expulsion of professors for a doctrine, by a prince, on a party's complaint.

The principle to recover is that a man under pressure must say what he believes. The Philippists' weakness before 1574 was ambiguity—holding the Reformed sense while subscribing formulas their colleagues read the Lutheran way—and the crisis simply ended the ambiguity. “no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5) is the standard. Pezel came out of it clearer than he went in, and gave Bremen a confession in plain words and a school to teach it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek koinonia (G2842), communion; Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad.

Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, a having in common; “the communion of the blood of Christ”, 1 Corinthians 10:16.

Greek poterion (G4221) — a cup; “The cup of blessing which we bless”, 1 Corinthians 10:16.

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad; “they were all scattered abroad”, Acts 8:1.

Greek aletheia (G225) — truth; “the truth of the gospel”, Galatians 2:5.

Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, to handle rightly; “rightly dividing the word of truth”, 2 Timothy 2:15.

Usage

"“The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1Co 10:16) — the doctrine for which he was expelled in 1574."

"“no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5) — the end of the Philippist ambiguity."

"“rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — the Bremen Consensus of 1595 and the city's high school."
